country.comment: Single-city case study of Delhi (National Capital Territory of Delhi) and its surrounding ring towns in India.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Introduction

effect_estimate.comment: No econometric or inferential effect estimate is computed; the paper presents descriptive institutional and documentary evidence across five axes of water exclusion using statutory text, Master Plans, PPP maps, and official audit/survey statistics.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported (descriptive documentary figures reported: Section 9(1a) of the DJB Act 1998 bars piped water supply to unlawfully constructed premises, excluding non-notified informal settlements where 5,716,000 residents or 33.62% of Delhi's population lived in 2014; in 2011–12, 24.8% of Delhi households lacked DJB piped connections and 3.25–3.42 million people relied on DJB tankers supplying 3.82 LPCD against the 172 LPCD official norm; lack of DDA–DJB coordination left planned Dwarka [pop. 1,000,000] without piped water for nearly 15 years until February 2015; 2018 Master Plan water norms ranged from 440–509 LPCD in elite NDMC/Cantonment zones to 40 LPCD in peripheral Outer Delhi; unconnected poor households buying DJB 20-L canisters via vendors paid Rs. 2,600/kl, 236 times Dwarka's Rs. 11/kl piped rate).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 4 and Table 1; PDF pp. 6–9 and Table 2; PDF pp. 10–12 and Tables 3–4; PDF p. 13, Table 5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling is 2 (non-experimental, non-ROBINS-I study). Assigned 2 because the paper directly documents concrete statutory, planning, spatial boundary, tariff, and inter-agency mechanisms operating on water access—including Section 9(1a) of the DJB Act 1998, explicit boundary carve-outs of slum pockets from the Mehrauli–Vasant Vihar 24x7 PPP (Figure 1), DDA building Dwarka without consulting DJB causing a 15-year delay in piped water, and tiered Master Plan LPCD/supply-hour standards.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6–13, Section 'Identifying Axes of Infrastructural Exclusion in Delhi'; PDF p. 13, Table 5

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory exclusion of non-notified slums and unauthorized settlements under DJB Act 1998 s. 9(1a) (tenure), tiered norms across Master Plans 1981/2001/2021 (planning), explicit spatial exclusion of slums from 24x7 PPP upgrade zones (service_area), canister/piped tariffs and user-pays pricing (fees), 15-year delay in piped supply to DDA sub-cities (delay), ad hoc tanker provision overlooking illegality under political and court pressure (accommodation, political_coordination, judicial_review), split DDA and DJB statutory mandates and non-consultation (institutional_fragmentation), disproportionate fining of informal settlements for water extraction alongside disconnections/evictions (sanction, disconnection), and RWA/community-driven management models (participation).

mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 6–13, Section 'Identifying Axes of Infrastructural Exclusion in Delhi'; PDF p. 13, Table 5; PDF p. 14, Section 'Discussion'

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes piped network connection exclusions (24.8% unconnected households), drinking water and community-toilet sanitation access, spatial service coverage and PPP boundary exclusions, irregular tanker reliability, LPCD/GPCD supply quantities (Tables 1, 3, 4), piped vs tanker vs canister water affordability, daily hours of supply (2–4 h, 12–24 h, 24x7), and 15-year delay in piped water delivery in Dwarka.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Selected per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because the study is a historical-institutional and legal/planning documentary analysis (statutes, court orders, Master Plans, PPP maps, and CAG audit reports) with no primary qualitative interview/ethnographic fieldwork protocol or quantitative primary survey design.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3; PDF pp. 6–13

sample_size.comment: No primary survey, household, or interview sample size is reported (apart from a passing unquantified mention of 'DJB officers' on PDF p. 8). The analysis draws on legislation (DJB Act 1998; DDA Act 1957), three Master Plans for Delhi (1981, 2001, 2021), and secondary official audit/statistical aggregates for Delhi (~17–20 million residents, including 15 DJB administrative divisions serving 3,253,840–3,421,630 residents via tankers in 2009–12 in Table 1, and 5,716,000 informal-settlement residents in 2014 in Table 2).
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 1–14 (full text inspected; secondary administrative aggregates in Table 1, PDF p. 4, and Table 2, PDF p. 7)

study_design.comment: Described by the authors as a 'historical and structured analysis' (PDF p. 3) applying the theoretical lens of infrastructural violence to Delhi's domestic water supply through colonial/post-colonial institutional history, statutory analysis (DJB Act 1998), urban planning document analysis (Master Plans for Delhi 1981, 2001, and 2021), PPP project mapping, and secondary audit/statistical data (CAG 2013, NSO 2018, Economic Survey of Delhi).
study_design.value: Historical-institutional and legal/planning documentary case study
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 'Infrastructural Violence in the World Class City'; PDF pp. 6–13, Section 'Identifying Axes of Infrastructural Exclusion in Delhi'

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 3, Section 'Infrastructural Violence in the World Class City'
evidence_quotes.quote: Through a historical and structured analysis, we aim to make a contribution to the theme of infrastructural violence by providing examples of how the relationships of hierarchy and power manifest to create inequitable access.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 4, Section 'Water Access and Marginalization in Delhi'
evidence_quotes.quote: A majority of these households were part of the unauthorized colonies and Jhuggi Jhopari clusters situated on the periphery of the city.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 7, Section 'Infrastructural Violence Through Legal Exclusion'
evidence_quotes.quote: But the main point is that legally speaking the DJB is not obliged to provide water to any illegally built residential areas, which include most of the unauthorized settlements and slums, where a large majority of Delhi residents live.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 7, Section 'Infrastructural Violence Through Commodification and Privatization'
evidence_quotes.quote: Corporate vendors sell 1 kl of water in canisters to the poor at the steep rate of Rs. 2,600 (Delhi Jal Board, 2015), which is 236 times higher than water supplied through the network.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 8, Section 'Infrastructural Violence Through Lack of Coordination'
evidence_quotes.quote: Dwarka got piped water supply from the DJB in February 2015 after nearly 15 years of the existence of the new town.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 11, Section 'Infrastructural Violence via City Planning'
evidence_quotes.quote: Some areas like the NDMC receive nearly 500 L of water per person per day in comparison to other areas only receiving 25 L per person per day.
